paper_topic: Citation-Consistent Voting (CCV): training-free permutation-robust RAG via document-ID agreement aggregation rather than answer frequency
anchor_paper: Wang et al., 2024 (Mixture-of-Agents majority voting baseline)

nodes.text: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving the factual accuracy of large language models by grounding responses in retrieved documents (Gao et al., 2023).
nodes.display_label: RAG grounds LLMs in retrieved docs

nodes.text: However, RAG systems exhibit a critical vulnerability: sensitivity to the ordering of retrieved documents.
nodes.display_label: RAG is sensitive to document ordering

nodes.text: Liu et al. (2023) demonstrated the "lost in the middle" phenomenon, where models struggle to utilize information positioned in the middle of the context.

More recently, Zhang et al. (2026) showed that even in short contexts with only five documents, merely permuting the document order can induce qualitatively different answers, including confident but incorrect responses.
Existing approaches to address this permutation sensitivity fall into two categories.
Training-based methods like Stable-RAG (Zhang et al., 2026) use preference optimization to make generators invariant to document ordering,
Inference-time methods like Mixture-of-Agents (Wang et al., 2024) generate multiple responses under different document orderings and aggregate via majority voting,
but require access to model weights and training data.
but this approach ignores the rich citation structure that modern RAG systems produce.
We observe that when language models cite evidence for their answers, the document they cite provides a more stable signal than the answer text itself.
nodes.display_label: citations are a more stable signal than answers

nodes.text: Our key insight is that correct answers tend to cite the same underlying document across permutations, while incorrect answers show more citation variance.
nodes.display_label: correct answers cite same doc across permutations

nodes.text: This motivates a new aggregation strategy: rather than voting on answer frequency, we vote on document-ID agreement among evidence-valid responses.
nodes.display_label: vote on document-ID agreement, not answer freq

nodes.text: We propose Citation-Consistent Voting (CCV), a training-free method that aggregates answers based on document-ID agreement rather than answer frequency.

CCV filters responses for evidence validity (ensuring the answer is grounded in the cited document), maps citations to permutation-invariant document IDs, and selects the answer with the highest citation-consistency score.
nodes.display_label: filter -> map to invariant doc IDs -> pick top score

nodes.text: We propose Citation-Consistent Voting, a training-free inference-time method for permutation-robust RAG that exploits citation structure for answer aggregation.
We demonstrate that CCV improves SubEM by +0.19 over majority voting on NaturalQuestions at K = 20 permutations, with gains scaling monotonically with K.
nodes.display_label: +0.19 SubEM vs majority vote, scales with K

nodes.text: We validate that document-ID agreement correlates significantly with answer correctness (p = 1.14 × 10−5 ), confirming that citation consistency is a meaningful quality signal.

N13 fans two addresses edges back to the two named Limitations, explicitly closing both gaps.

Anchor paper: Wang et al. 2024 (Mixture-of-Agents) is the inference-time baseline that CCV directly replaces. Zhang et al. 2026 (Stable-RAG) is the comparison training-based method.

Strong lexical overlap supports the addresses edges: N13 'training-free' resolves N6 'require ... training data', and N13 'exploits citation structure' shares 'citation structure' verbatim with N7.
